Lecture notes

Purpose of this week

This first week is designed to orient students to the course, the learning platform, and the role of GIS in hydrology. Students should come away understanding not only the logistics of the class, but also why spatial thinking is fundamental to water resources analysis. The first week sets expectations for how we will work, how assignments will be completed, and how GIS will support hydrologic reasoning throughout the course.

Course syllabus

The syllabus is your guide for the entire course. It explains what topics will be covered, how you will be graded, when assignments are due, and what skills you are expected to develop. You should read it carefully at the beginning of the course and return to it throughout the term.

Student survey responses

You may have completed a survey about your background and experience. This helps tailor the course to match the range of student skills. In GIS and hydrology, students often have different levels of experience with maps, data, and software, so this information helps ensure the course is appropriately paced and supported.

Canvas and Slack

The course is fully online, so the learning platform (Canvas) is where everything happens. You should become familiar with where to find:

  • lecture slides and notes
  • lab instructions
  • assignments and submission links
  • announcements and updates

In addition to Canvas, I have also hosted a slack channel for the class. In the past students have found this outlet to be effective at discussions and problem solving among each other and it’s a platform I can constantly check and may have quicker response times than email. You are free to email me and the TA questions or post them there. Keep in mind that you all are encouraged to work together and help each other problem solve. So the TA (Kyrian) and I will not usually answer questions right away, we will sit back and observe the thread for a while and act as facilitators to help guide you all reaching the answer rather than just posting it.

Tips and tricks

GIS involves working with many files, datasets, and tools. Staying organized from the beginning is critical. Keep your files clearly named and stored in logical folders. Small mistakes—such as using the wrong dataset or coordinate system—can lead to incorrect results.

It is also normal to feel overwhelmed at first. GIS skills build over time through practice.

Introduction to GIS for Hydrology

Hydrology is the study of how water moves through the environment, including rainfall, runoff, infiltration, and streamflow. These processes are strongly influenced by spatial factors such as elevation, land cover, soil type, and watershed boundaries.

GIS (Geographic Information Systems) is a tool that allows us to analyze these spatial relationships. It helps answer questions such as:

Where does water flow across a landscape?

How large is a watershed?

How does land use affect runoff and water quality?

Throughout this course, GIS will be used to connect physical processes to real-world data.

Lab examples

Labs are where you will apply what you learn. Instead of just reading about GIS and hydrology, you will work directly with spatial datasets and software.

In labs, you may:

  • explore maps and spatial layers
  • analyze elevation and watershed data
  • create your own maps
  • interpret results in a hydrologic context

The goal is not just to complete steps, but to understand what the results mean.

Cartography basics and class expectations

Cartography is the practice of making clear and effective maps. A good map communicates information quickly and accurately.

You will learn how to:

  • choose appropriate colors and symbols
  • label features clearly
  • design maps that are easy to interpret

In this course, you are expected to produce maps that are both technically correct and visually clear.

Why this matters in hydrology

Hydrology is inherently spatial. Water movement depends on landscape features such as slope, drainage networks, and land use. GIS allows you to analyze these relationships in a structured and reproducible way.

The skills you begin learning in Week 1—organization, spatial thinking, and map interpretation—are foundational for all future work in water resources, environmental science, and engineering.

Key takeaway

Week 1 sets the foundation for the course by helping you understand how the class works and introducing GIS as a core tool for analyzing hydrologic systems.

Slide 5 GIS in Water Resources

On the slide

  • Course goal: learn advanced GIS applications to resolve water resource issues
  • Hydrologists and GIS specialists use many data sources, software programs, and models
  • GIS integrates these diverse datasets in one spatial framework

Lecture notes

Goal – Learn advanced GIS applications to resolve water resource issues

The primary goal of this course is not just to learn GIS tools, but to apply them to real-world water resource challenges. These challenges include problems such as flooding, water supply management, drought, water quality, and ecosystem health.

“Advanced applications” means moving beyond basic map-making to using GIS for:

  • spatial analysis
  • watershed delineation
  • hydrologic modeling support
  • interpreting environmental datasets
  • decision-making and planning

By the end of the course, you should be able to use GIS as a problem-solving tool, not just a visualization tool.

Hydrologists and GIS specialists use many different data sources, software programs, and models

Water resource analysis is inherently interdisciplinary and data-intensive. Professionals in this field rarely rely on a single dataset or tool.

Common types of data include:

  • precipitation and climate data
  • streamflow and gauge records
  • digital elevation models (DEMs)
  • land cover and land use data
  • soil properties
  • groundwater data

In addition, multiple tools are often used together, such as:

  • GIS software (e.g., ArcGIS, QGIS)
  • hydrologic models (e.g., HEC-HMS, PRMS)
  • hydraulic models (e.g., HEC-RAS)
  • statistical and programming tools (e.g., Python, R)

This means that a key skill in water resources is not just using one tool, but understanding how different tools and datasets connect.

GIS provides the capability to integrate various data

One of the most powerful aspects of GIS is its ability to bring different types of data into a common spatial framework.

For example, GIS allows you to combine:

  • elevation data (to understand slope and flow direction)
  • land cover (to estimate runoff or infiltration)
  • soil data (to evaluate water storage and permeability)
  • climate data (to assess precipitation patterns)

By layering these datasets together, GIS helps answer complex questions such as:

How will land use change affect runoff?

Which areas contribute most to flooding?

Where are critical zones for groundwater recharge?

How might climate change impact watershed behavior?

Without GIS, integrating these datasets would be extremely difficult and time-consuming.

Why this matters in hydrology

Hydrologic systems are controlled by spatial variability. Water does not move uniformly across a landscape—it follows topography, responds to land cover, and interacts with soils and geology.

GIS allows hydrologists to:

  • analyze watersheds as interconnected systems
  • quantify spatial relationships (e.g., slope, drainage area)
  • support modeling and prediction
  • communicate findings through maps and visualizations

In professional practice, nearly every hydrologic analysis involves some level of GIS.

Slide 13 How Labs Are Graded: Three Criteria

On the slide

  • Grades for labs will depend on three things:

Lecture notes

Accuracy

Accuracy refers to whether your answers and analyses are correct.

This includes:

  • correctly applying GIS tools and methods
  • producing correct outputs (e.g., watershed boundaries, flow paths, calculations)
  • answering questions using appropriate reasoning
  • interpreting results correctly

Accuracy is critical because hydrologic analyses often inform real-world decisions. Errors in analysis—such as incorrect watershed delineation or misinterpreting flow accumulation—can lead to incorrect conclusions about water movement, flood risk, or resource management.

Completeness

Completeness refers to whether you have finished all parts of the assignment and followed instructions fully.

This includes:

  • answering every question
  • submitting all required deliverables
  • including units where appropriate
  • following formatting or submission requirements
  • turning in assignments on time

In GIS workflows, missing even a single step can make results unusable or difficult to interpret. Completeness ensures your work is functional and usable.

Design

Design refers to the quality and clarity of your maps and visual outputs.

This includes:

  • whether maps are easy to understand
  • clear labeling of features and data
  • appropriate color choices and symbology
  • inclusion of essential map elements (legend, scale, title)
  • overall visual clarity and professionalism

A technically correct analysis is not enough if it is not communicated clearly. In hydrology and water resources, maps are often used to communicate findings to decision-makers, stakeholders, or the public. Poor design can obscure important information.

Slide 18 Introduction to GIS for Hydrology

On the slide

  • Understanding Data
  • Data Types
  • Hydrology vs. Hydrography
  • Data Sources

Lecture notes

Data Types

GIS uses different types of data structures, each suited for different types of analysis.

The two primary types are:

  • Raster data: grid-based data (e.g., elevation, precipitation, temperature)
  • Vector data: point, line, and polygon features (e.g., stream gauges, rivers, watershed boundaries)

In hydrology:

  • raster data is often used for continuous variables like elevation and rainfall
  • vector data is used for discrete features like streams and monitoring stations

Understanding when and how to use each type is fundamental to performing correct analyses.

Hydrology vs. Hydrography

These two terms are related but distinct.

Hydrology is the science of water movement and processes, including precipitation, runoff, infiltration, evapotranspiration, and streamflow.

Hydrography refers to the mapping and description of water features, such as rivers, lakes, and coastlines.

In GIS:

  • hydrology focuses on modeling and analyzing processes
  • hydrography focuses on representing physical water features

For example, a stream network dataset is hydrography, while flow accumulation derived from a DEM is part of hydrologic analysis.

Data Sources

Hydrologic GIS analyses rely on data from many different sources.

Common sources include:

  • government agencies (e.g., USGS, NOAA, EPA)
  • satellite and remote sensing products
  • field measurements (e.g., stream gauges, weather stations)
  • modeled datasets (e.g., climate projections, hydrologic simulations)

Each data source has its own strengths and limitations. Selecting appropriate data is a critical step in any analysis.

Why this matters in hydrology

Hydrologic analyses depend heavily on data quality and interpretation. Misunderstanding data types or sources can lead to incorrect conclusions about watershed behavior.

For example:

  • using low-resolution elevation data may misrepresent drainage patterns
  • confusing hydrography (mapped streams) with hydrologic flow paths can lead to errors in analysis
  • using inappropriate data sources may reduce the reliability of results

A strong understanding of data is essential for building accurate and defensible hydrologic analyses.

Slide 19 Tips & Tricks (“Gotchas”)

On the slide

  • In GIS there are always multiple ways to do something — but simple things can stop you in your tracks
  • Slow down and follow instructions. Beginners can be “click happy” — be patient
  • Avoid spaces in file paths; work on a local drive; back up your data
  • Esri GRID rasters outside a geodatabase: names of 13 characters or fewer (or use GeoTIFF)
  • Check your projection, coordinate system, and units!
  • Read the metadata (if available)
  • Use ArcGIS Help! Google it! Ask your colleagues!

Lecture notes

There are many ways to do things in GIS

GIS is a flexible tool, and there are often multiple ways to achieve the same result. While this flexibility is powerful, it can also be confusing. Small mistakes—such as selecting the wrong input file or tool parameter—can cause workflows to fail or produce incorrect results.

Because of this, attention to detail is essential.

Slow down and follow instructions

When learning GIS, it is common to click through tools quickly without fully understanding each step. This often leads to errors.

Instead:

  • carefully read instructions before running a tool
  • double-check inputs and settings
  • take time to understand what each step is doing

Developing a careful workflow early will save time later.

File paths, local drives, and backups

GIS software can be sensitive to how files are stored.

Best practices include:

  • avoid spaces or overly complex file paths when possible
  • work on a local drive instead of network or cloud drives to prevent performance issues
  • regularly back up your data to avoid losing work

File organization is a critical part of successful GIS work.

GRID naming limitations

Some raster formats (especially older Esri GRID formats) have strict naming rules, such as limits on the number of characters.

If naming rules are not followed:

  • tools may fail without clear error messages
  • outputs may not be created correctly

Using simple, short, and consistent file names helps avoid these issues.

Check projection, coordinate system, and units

Spatial data must be in a consistent coordinate system to work correctly together.

Always verify:

  • projection (e.g., geographic vs. projected)
  • coordinate system (e.g., WGS84, UTM)
  • units (e.g., meters, feet)

Mismatched coordinate systems can cause layers to appear in the wrong location or produce incorrect measurements (e.g., area, distance, slope).

Read metadata (if available)

Metadata describes how a dataset was created, including:

  • data source
  • resolution
  • accuracy
  • processing steps

Reading metadata helps you understand whether a dataset is appropriate for your analysis and how reliable it is.

Use help resources

Learning GIS often involves troubleshooting. You are encouraged to use available resources:

  • ArcGIS Help documentation
  • online searches (e.g., forums, tutorials)
  • classmates or colleagues

Being able to find answers and solve problems independently is an important skill in GIS.

Slide 20 Understanding Data: Four Levels of Abstraction

On the slide

  • Conceptual Model
  • Mathematical Model
  • Data Model
  • Geographic Data Model

Lecture notes

Understanding data means understanding the chain of abstraction from the real world to a GIS database. We will step through four levels: a conceptual model, a mathematical model, a data model, and a geographic data model. Each level builds on the one before it.

Slide 21 Understanding Data: Conceptual Model

On the slide

  • Conceptual Model
    • a set of concepts that describe a subject and allow reasoning about it

Lecture notes

What is a conceptual model?

A conceptual model is a set of concepts and relationships that describe how a system works. It allows us to organize our thinking about a subject before we begin working with data or equations.

Rather than focusing on numbers or software, a conceptual model focuses on:

  • key components of a system
  • how those components interact
  • cause-and-effect relationships

It is essentially a mental or visual framework for understanding a problem.

Conceptual models in hydrology

In hydrology, conceptual models are used to describe how water moves through the environment.

For example, a simple conceptual model of a watershed might include:

  • precipitation falling on the landscape
  • some water infiltrating into the soil
  • some water becoming surface runoff
  • water flowing into streams and rivers
  • evaporation and transpiration returning water to the atmosphere

This model helps you understand the system before applying GIS tools or mathematical equations.

Why conceptual models come first

Before working with GIS or hydrologic models, you need to understand what you are trying to represent.

If you skip this step:

  • you may choose the wrong data
  • you may misuse GIS tools
  • you may misinterpret results

A strong conceptual model helps guide:

  • what data you need
  • what analyses to perform
  • how to interpret outputs

The image on this slide shows how conceptual thinking connects to data representation in GIS.

It illustrates that:

  • real-world phenomena are translated into data structures
  • these structures include raster (grids), vector (features), or object-based models
  • each representation stores values or attributes that describe the system

This means that before choosing a raster or vector dataset, you should first think conceptually about what you are trying to represent.

Slide 22 Understanding Data: Mathematical Model

On the slide

  • Mathematical Model
    • A conceptual model expressed through equations, statistics, etc.

Lecture notes

What is a mathematical model?

A mathematical model is a conceptual model that has been translated into equations, formulas, or statistical relationships.

While a conceptual model describes how a system works, a mathematical model describes it in a way that can be calculated and analyzed.

For example:

  • instead of saying “more rainfall leads to more runoff,”
  • a mathematical model defines exactly how much runoff results from a given amount of rainfall

Types of mathematical models in hydrology

Hydrologic mathematical models can take many forms, including:

Empirical/statistical models

Based on observed data and relationships (e.g., regression models, interpolation methods)

Process-based models

Based on physical laws (e.g., conservation of mass, energy, momentum)

Deterministic models

Produce the same output for a given input

Stochastic models

Incorporate randomness and uncertainty

These models are used to simulate processes such as:

  • rainfall-runoff relationships
  • streamflow generation
  • groundwater flow
  • sediment transport

Example shown on this slide (rainfall interpolation)

The map on this slide shows rainfall across Southeast Portland estimated using spline interpolation.

In this case:

  • rainfall measurements are collected at specific gauge locations (points)
  • a mathematical method (interpolation) is used to estimate rainfall values between those points
  • the result is a continuous surface (raster) showing spatial variation in rainfall

This is an example of a mathematical model because:

  • it uses equations to estimate unknown values
  • it transforms discrete data into a continuous spatial dataset

Why mathematical models are important in GIS

GIS often relies on mathematical models to:

  • fill gaps in data (e.g., interpolation)
  • estimate spatial patterns
  • simulate hydrologic processes
  • support decision-making

Many GIS tools you will use—such as flow accumulation or slope calculation—are based on underlying mathematical relationships.

Slide 23 Understanding Data: Data Model

On the slide

  • Data Model
    • a conceptual model expressed in a data structure (e.g., ASCII files, Excel tables, databases)

Lecture notes

What is a data model?

A data model is a way of organizing and structuring information so that it can be stored and used in analysis.

It takes a conceptual understanding of a system and represents it in a format that computers can work with.

Examples of data structures include:

  • spreadsheets (e.g., Excel tables)
  • text-based formats (e.g., ASCII files)
  • databases
  • GIS datasets

A data model defines:

  • how data is stored
  • how different pieces of data are related
  • how data can be accessed and analyzed

From conceptual model to data model

A conceptual model describes how a system works, but it is not directly usable in GIS or software.

A data model translates that understanding into structured data.

For example:

  • Conceptual idea: “a river flows through a watershed”

Data model representation:

  • river → stored as a line feature
  • watershed → stored as a polygon
  • attributes → stored in tables (e.g., flow rate, area)

This translation allows us to perform analysis using GIS tools.

Example shown on this slide (real world → vector and raster)

The image on this slide shows how the real world can be represented using different data models.

Vector representation

Uses points, lines, and polygons

Represents discrete features such as roads, rivers, and boundaries

Stores attributes in tables

Raster representation

Uses a grid of cells (pixels)

Represents continuous surfaces such as elevation, rainfall, or temperature

Each cell contains a value

Both representations are abstractions of reality. Neither is “perfect”—each is suited for different types of analysis.

Choosing the right data model

The choice of data model depends on the type of data and analysis.

Use vector for:

  • discrete features (e.g., stream networks, monitoring stations)
  • boundaries (e.g., watersheds, land parcels)

Use raster for:

  • continuous variables (e.g., elevation, precipitation)
  • surface-based analysis (e.g., slope, flow direction)

Understanding this distinction is essential for selecting appropriate tools and interpreting results correctly.

Slide 24 Understanding Data: Geographic Data Model

On the slide

  • Geographic Data Model
    • a conceptual model for describing and reasoning about the world expressed in a GIS database

Lecture notes

What is a geographic data model?

A geographic data model is a way of representing real-world features and processes in a GIS database so that they can be analyzed spatially.

It combines:

  • conceptual understanding of the real world
  • structured data formats (vector and raster)
  • spatial relationships between features

In other words, it is how GIS “thinks about” the world.

Layer-based representation (image on slide)

The image shows a key concept in GIS: layering.

The real world is complex, but GIS breaks it into separate layers, such as:

  • imagery (aerial or satellite images)
  • elevation (terrain)
  • transportation (roads)
  • boundaries (political or watershed)
  • water features (rivers, lakes)
  • survey/control points
  • user-generated data

Each layer represents one aspect of reality. These layers can be stacked and analyzed together.

Why layering is powerful

By organizing data into layers, GIS allows you to:

  • combine multiple datasets
  • analyze relationships between different variables
  • isolate specific features when needed
  • build complex analyses step by step

For example, in hydrology, you might combine:

  • elevation (to determine flow direction)
  • land cover (to estimate runoff)
  • soil data (to evaluate infiltration)
  • stream networks (to trace water movement)

Spatial relationships

A key feature of the geographic data model is that it preserves spatial relationships, such as:

  • proximity (how close features are)
  • connectivity (how features are linked, such as streams)
  • containment (what lies within a boundary, such as a watershed)

These relationships are essential for hydrologic analysis.

GIS database structure

All of these layers are stored in a GIS database (often called a geodatabase), which organizes:

  • spatial data (location and geometry)
  • attribute data (descriptive information)
  • relationships between datasets

This structure allows efficient storage, retrieval, and analysis of geographic information.

Slide 25 Geographic Data Model: An Inventory of Layers

On the slide

  • Based on an inventory of data layers
  • Often used in multi-criteria analysis — e.g., combining terrain, rainfall, and land cover to map runoff potential

Lecture notes

Inventory of data layers

In GIS, an “inventory of data layers” means collecting and organizing all relevant spatial datasets needed for an analysis.

For hydrologic applications, this often includes layers such as:

  • stream networks
  • hydrographic points (e.g., gauge stations)
  • drainage areas (watersheds)
  • channel networks
  • terrain or elevation (DEM)
  • rainfall or climate data
  • aerial imagery

Each layer represents a different aspect of the system. Individually, they provide partial information. Together, they provide a more complete understanding.

Layer stack shown on the slide

The image illustrates how different types of hydrologic and geographic data are stacked:

  • Digital orthophotography → real-world imagery
  • Rainfall response → how precipitation varies spatially
  • Surface terrain (DEM) → controls flow direction and slope
  • Channels and hydrography → represent water pathways
  • Drainage areas → define watershed boundaries
  • Hydrographic points → monitoring locations (e.g., gauges)
  • Streams → surface water network

This layered structure allows GIS to integrate diverse datasets into a unified framework.

Multi-criteria analysis

Multi-criteria analysis involves combining multiple data layers to evaluate a problem based on several factors.

In hydrology, this might include:

  • identifying flood-prone areas using elevation, rainfall, and land use
  • selecting suitable locations for water infrastructure
  • evaluating watershed sensitivity to land use change
  • prioritizing restoration areas

Each layer contributes a piece of information, and GIS allows you to overlay and analyze them together.

How layers interact

The power of GIS comes from analyzing how layers relate to one another.

For example:

  • rainfall + slope + land cover → runoff potential
  • elevation + flow direction → watershed boundaries
  • streams + drainage areas → hydrologic connectivity

By combining layers, you can move from simple visualization to deeper analysis and interpretation.

Why this matters in hydrology

Water resource problems are rarely driven by a single factor. Instead, they are influenced by multiple interacting variables across space.

For example:

  • flood risk depends on terrain, rainfall, and land use
  • water quality depends on land cover, soils, and flow paths
  • groundwater recharge depends on soil properties, slope, and precipitation

GIS allows hydrologists to analyze these interactions in a structured and spatially explicit way.

Slide 26 Data Types: Vector vs. Raster

On the slide

  • Two Main Types in GIS
    • Vector
    • Raster

Lecture notes

Two main types in GIS

All spatial data in GIS is generally represented using one of two formats:

  • vector data
  • raster data

Each type represents the real world differently and is suited for different types of analysis.

Vector data

Vector data represents features as discrete objects using geometry.

There are three main types:

  • Points → single locations (e.g., rain gauges, wells)
  • Lines → linear features (e.g., rivers, streams, channels)
  • Polygons → areas (e.g., watersheds, lakes, land parcels)

Vector data is best used when:

  • boundaries are clearly defined
  • features are discrete and countable
  • high precision is needed

For example, a watershed boundary is best represented as a polygon, and a stream network as lines.

Vector data also includes attribute tables, which store additional information such as flow rate, name, or classification.

Raster data

Raster data represents the world as a grid of cells (pixels), where each cell has a value.

Raster data is best used for continuous variables such as:

  • elevation (DEM)
  • precipitation
  • temperature
  • land surface properties

Each cell represents a value at a specific location. The resolution (cell size) determines how detailed the data is.

For example:

  • a DEM uses raster data to represent terrain elevation
  • rainfall maps use raster data to show spatial variation

Vector vs. raster (comparison)

The image on this slide highlights key differences:

Vector data:

  • smooth, precise boundaries
  • efficient for discrete features
  • easier to associate with attribute tables

Raster data:

  • grid-based representation
  • ideal for surface analysis
  • required for many hydrologic tools (e.g., flow direction, slope)

Neither format is better overall—they serve different purposes.

Choosing the right data type

The choice depends on your analysis goal.

In hydrology:

use vector for:

  • stream networks
  • watershed boundaries
  • monitoring locations

use raster for:

  • terrain analysis
  • flow modeling
  • rainfall and climate surfaces

Many analyses require both types working together.

Slide 27 Spatial Data: Vector Format

On the slide

  • Vector data are defined spatially in three ways:
  • Point - a pair of X and Y coordinates (& maybe Z)
  • Line - a sequence of points
  • Polygon - a closed set of lines

Figure 18 (diagram). Point example: a single dot labeled with coordinates (x1, y1, z1).

Figure 19 (diagram). Polygon example: a closed five-sided shape formed by connected line segments.

Figure 20 (diagram). Line example: a zig-zag line whose end points are labeled “node” and whose interior bend point is labeled “vertex.”

Lecture notes

Vector data representation

Vector data represents real-world features using coordinates. Each feature is defined by its geometry (shape and location) and associated attributes (descriptive information).

There are three primary types of vector geometry:

Point

A point represents a single location in space, defined by coordinates.

Typically expressed as (X, Y), and sometimes (X, Y, Z) if elevation is included

Has no length or area

Examples in hydrology:

  • rain gauges
  • streamflow monitoring stations
  • wells

Points are used when the feature is small relative to the map scale or when only location matters.

Line (or polyline)

A line is made up of a sequence of connected points.

Represents length but not area

Defined by vertices (points along the line)

Examples in hydrology:

  • rivers and streams
  • flow paths
  • canals or pipelines

Lines are important for representing connectivity, such as how water flows through a network.

Polygon

A polygon is a closed shape made up of connected lines.

Represents an area

Must form a closed boundary

Examples in hydrology:

  • watershed boundaries
  • lakes and reservoirs
  • flood zones

Polygons are used when area and boundaries are important.

Vertices and nodes

The image on this slide shows how vector features are constructed:

  • Vertices are the points that define the shape of a line or polygon
  • Nodes are endpoints or connection points in a network

These elements are critical for defining geometry and spatial relationships.

For example:

  • more vertices → more detailed representation of a river
  • fewer vertices → simpler, less detailed geometry

Attributes in vector data

In addition to geometry, vector data includes attribute tables.

These tables store information such as:

  • stream name
  • flow rate
  • watershed area
  • classification or type

This allows vector data to combine spatial and descriptive information.

Slide 28 Spatial Data: Raster Format

On the slide

  • Point
  • Line
  • Polygon
  • Vector
  • Raster
  • Raster data: a grid of cells, one value per cell

Figure 21 (diagram). Vector line: a straight line.

Figure 22 (diagram). Vector point: a single small dot.

Figure 23 (diagram). Raster point: a single grid cell.

Figure 24 (diagram). Raster polygon: a 3-by-3 block of grid cells.

Figure 25 (diagram). Raster line: a row of five grid cells.

Figure 26 (diagram). Vector polygon: a rounded square outline.

Lecture notes

What is raster data?

Raster data represents the world as a grid of equally sized cells (pixels), where each cell contains a single value.

Key characteristics:

  • continuous surface representation
  • one value per cell
  • organized in rows and columns

Each value represents a measurement or category at that location.

Examples:

  • elevation (DEM) → elevation value per cell
  • rainfall → precipitation amount per cell
  • temperature → temperature value per cell

How raster represents features (diagram on slide)

The diagram shows how raster represents features differently than vector:

  • A point becomes a single cell
  • A line becomes a series of connected cells
  • A polygon becomes a block of cells

Unlike vector data, raster does not store exact boundaries—it approximates them using grid cells.

Continuous vs. discrete representation

Raster is best suited for continuous surfaces, where values change gradually across space.

Examples of continuous data:

  • elevation
  • rainfall
  • soil moisture
  • temperature

Vector is better for discrete features, where boundaries are clearly defined.

Examples:

  • rivers
  • watershed boundaries
  • infrastructure

Resolution and cell size

An important concept in raster data is resolution, which refers to the size of each cell.

smaller cell size → higher resolution (more detail, larger file size)

larger cell size → lower resolution (less detail, smaller file size)

Resolution affects:

  • accuracy of analysis
  • level of detail in outputs
  • computational performance

For example, a coarse DEM may miss small drainage features, while a high-resolution DEM captures finer terrain detail.

Why raster is important in GIS and hydrology

Many GIS analyses rely on raster data because it supports surface-based calculations.

Common raster-based analyses include:

  • slope and aspect calculation
  • flow direction and flow accumulation
  • watershed delineation
  • interpolation of environmental variables

These analyses depend on having continuous data across space.

Slide 29 Data Layers (Themes) and Their Data Types

On the slide

  • Each layer is stored as vector (point, line, polygon) or raster data
  • Line
  • Point
  • Polygon
  • Line/Polygon
  • Line/Polygon
  • Raster
  • Raster
  • Raster

Lecture notes

This slide pairs each data layer with how it is typically stored. Streams are lines; hydrographic points such as gauges are points; drainage areas are polygons; hydrography and channels can be lines or polygons; and surface terrain, rainfall response, and orthophotography are rasters. Most hydrologic projects combine vector and raster layers.

Slide 30 Data Layers in the ArcGIS Table of Contents

Figure 29 (diagram). Red arrow pointing to the Table of Contents.

Lecture notes

The screenshot shows the ArcGIS interface with a Table of Contents, which lists all the layers in the map.

Key points:

  • each layer is stacked on top of others
  • the order of layers affects what is visible
  • layers can be symbolized differently (colors, shading, transparency)
  • multiple layers can be displayed simultaneously

For example, in the image:

  • a stream layer (blue lines) is shown
  • floodplain or elevation layers are shaded underneath
  • a base map provides background context

Layer stacking and visualization

Layers are drawn from bottom to top:

  • base layers (e.g., imagery or terrain) are typically at the bottom
  • analysis layers (e.g., flood extents, streams) are placed above

Transparency can be used so multiple layers are visible at once.

This allows you to visually interpret relationships between datasets.

Using layers for analysis

Layers are not just for visualization—they are the foundation of GIS analysis.

You can:

  • overlay layers to find relationships
  • extract information from one layer using another
  • combine layers to create new datasets

For example:

  • overlaying floodplain data with infrastructure → identify at-risk areas
  • combining elevation and rainfall → estimate runoff patterns

Attribute data within layers

Each layer also contains attribute information.

For example:

  • a stream layer may include flow data or stream order
  • a floodplain layer may include depth or frequency information

This allows both spatial and numerical analysis.

Slide 31 Attributes Linked to Features

Figure 31 (diagram). Red arrow pointing from the selected map feature to its row in the attribute table.

Lecture notes

What is an attribute table?

An attribute table is a tabular dataset associated with a spatial layer. Each row represents a feature, and each column represents a property (attribute) of that feature.

For example:

  • one row = one polygon (e.g., a floodplain area)
  • columns = characteristics such as area, name, land type, or description

This allows GIS to store both where something is and what it is.

Structure of the table (image on slide)

The table shown includes several common fields:

  • OBJECTID → unique identifier for each feature
  • Shape → geometry type (e.g., polygon)
  • Area / Acres → size of the feature
  • Name → label or identifier
  • Description → type or classification (e.g., riparian forest, wetlands)
  • Bounds → location or reference description

Each row corresponds to a specific mapped feature, such as a wetland or riparian zone.

Link between map and table

One of the most important concepts in GIS is that spatial features are linked to attribute data.

This means:

  • selecting a feature on the map highlights its row in the table
  • selecting a row in the table highlights the feature on the map

This connection allows you to move between spatial and descriptive analysis.

Slide 32 How Do You Combine These Data?

On the slide

  • DEMs
  • Watersheds
  • Streams

Lecture notes

How these datasets are connected

These datasets are not created independently—they are derived from one another, primarily starting with the DEM.

Step 1: Start with the DEM (surface topography)

The DEM provides information about elevation and slope. Since water flows downhill, elevation controls the direction and accumulation of flow.

Step 2: Derive flow direction and flow accumulation

Using the DEM, GIS tools calculate:

  • flow direction → where water moves from each cell
  • flow accumulation → how much water flows into each location

These are raster-based calculations.

Step 3: Delineate stream networks

Streams are typically derived by identifying areas with high flow accumulation.

cells with large contributing area → likely stream locations

converted into vector lines for stream networks

Step 4: Delineate watersheds

Watersheds are defined based on flow direction and outlet points.

GIS traces all upstream areas contributing to a point

resulting in polygon boundaries representing drainage areas

Step 5: Establish connectivity

Once streams and watersheds are derived, GIS can analyze relationships such as:

  • which streams belong to which watershed
  • how watersheds are connected upstream and downstream
  • how water flows through the network

Slide 33 An Integrated Raster–Vector Geodatabase

On the slide

  • Arc Hydro Tools

Lecture notes

What is an integrated raster–vector geodatabase?

An integrated geodatabase is a structured GIS database that stores and connects multiple types of spatial data, including:

  • Raster data → elevation, flow direction, flow accumulation
  • Vector data → streams, watersheds, catchments, monitoring points

Rather than treating these datasets separately, they are linked together so they can support a complete hydrologic workflow.

Why integration is important

Hydrologic analysis requires both raster and vector data because they represent different aspects of the system:

  • raster data (e.g., DEMs) → represent continuous surfaces and processes
  • vector data (e.g., streams, watersheds) → represent discrete features and networks

An integrated system allows:

  • raster analysis to generate vector features
  • vector features to be linked back to raster-derived properties
  • consistent relationships across datasets

Arc Hydro Tools

Arc Hydro is a set of tools designed to support hydrologic analysis within GIS.

It provides:

  • standardized workflows for processing DEMs
  • tools for generating streams and watersheds
  • data structures for organizing hydrologic information
  • relationships between raster and vector datasets

Arc Hydro helps ensure that datasets are:

  • consistent
  • properly linked
  • ready for analysis and modeling

Slide 34 Arc Hydro: GIS for Water Resources

On the slide

  • The Arc Hydro data model and application tools are in the public domain
  • Today: Arc Hydro Tools Pro — a free download for ArcGIS Pro
  • Published by Esri Press

Lecture notes

Arc Hydro, edited by David Maidment and published by Esri Press in 2002, defined a standard data model and toolset for water resources GIS. The data model and tools are freely available, and Arc Hydro Tools Pro is the current version for ArcGIS Pro. Many of the workflows in this course follow Arc Hydro concepts.

Slide 35 A Data Model Based on Behavior: Follow the Water

On the slide

  • “Follow a drop of water from where it falls on the land, to the stream, and all the way to the ocean.”
  • R.M. Hirsch, USGS

Lecture notes

The quote on this slide captures a fundamental principle in hydrology:

Follow a drop of water from where it falls on the land, to the stream, and all the way to the ocean.

This means we are not just mapping features—we are trying to understand how water moves through the system.

This movement includes:

  • precipitation falling on the land surface
  • infiltration into the soil
  • overland flow (runoff)
  • flow into streams and rivers
  • downstream transport to larger water bodies

From static data to dynamic behavior

Earlier, we discussed data types (raster, vector) and layers (streams, watersheds, DEMs). Those represent what exists.

This slide shifts the focus to:

  • what happens
  • how things are connected through flow

For example:

  • a DEM is not just elevation—it determines how water flows
  • a stream network is not just lines—it represents pathways of water movement
  • a watershed is not just a boundary—it defines contributing flow areas

Behavior-based data modeling

A behavior-based model organizes data around processes, especially flow and connectivity.

In GIS hydrology, this includes:

  • flow direction grids (where water moves)
  • flow accumulation (how much water contributes to a point)
  • stream networks (paths of concentrated flow)
  • watershed delineation (areas contributing to a point)

These datasets are linked because they describe the same process: water movement.

Slide 36 Integrating Data Using a Behavioral Model

On the slide

  • Relationships between objects linked by tracing path of water movement

Figure 40 (diagram). Diagram: seven stacked data layers joined by vertical red lines, showing that a location on each layer is linked to the same location on the others by tracing the path of water.

Lecture notes

Behavioral model approach

A behavioral model organizes data based on how the system functions, rather than just how it is stored.

In hydrology, the key behavior is:

  • how water moves across the landscape

This means we connect datasets based on:

  • flow direction
  • upstream–downstream relationships
  • drainage connectivity

Linking layers through water movement

The diagram shows multiple layers stacked vertically, representing different datasets.

The vertical red lines represent connections between layers, created by following the path of water.

This means:

  • a location on the landscape is connected across multiple datasets
  • relationships are defined by how water flows through those locations

For example:

  • a point on a stream is linked to its upstream watershed
  • a watershed is linked to the terrain that generates runoff
  • land surface properties influence flow behavior

Relationships between objects

GIS allows us to establish relationships between spatial features.

Examples include:

  • which watershed contributes flow to a stream segment
  • which upstream areas affect a downstream location
  • how different layers influence one another

These relationships are not arbitrary—they are based on physical processes.

Why tracing water movement is key

Water movement provides a natural way to connect datasets.

By tracing flow paths, GIS can:

  • link raster and vector data
  • establish connectivity across layers
  • support modeling and analysis

This is what allows GIS to move from simple mapping to process-based analysis.

Slide 37 Arc Hydro Components

On the slide

  • Flow
  • Time
  • Time Series
  • Hydrography
  • Hydro Network
  • Channel System
  • Drainage System

Lecture notes

Overview of Arc Hydro components

Arc Hydro is designed to represent hydrologic systems as a set of interconnected elements. The main components shown here are:

  • Drainage System
  • Hydro Network
  • Hydrography
  • Channel System
  • Time Series

Each component represents a different way of describing water in the landscape.

Drainage System (watersheds)

The drainage system represents watershed boundaries—areas where all water drains to a common outlet.

Key characteristics:

  • represented as polygons
  • defines contributing areas
  • used for summarizing hydrologic properties (e.g., area, runoff)

Watersheds provide the spatial context for understanding where water comes from.

Hydro Network (connectivity)

The hydro network represents the connectivity of streams.

Key characteristics:

  • network of connected stream segments
  • includes nodes (junctions) and links (stream segments)
  • supports upstream/downstream tracing

This allows GIS to answer questions such as:

what areas contribute flow to a location?

what is downstream of a point?

Hydrography (mapped water features)

Hydrography refers to the mapped representation of water features.

Includes:

  • rivers and streams
  • lakes and water bodies
  • drainage features

This is often based on observed or mapped data rather than derived from DEMs.

Channel System (flow pathways and geometry)

The channel system represents the physical structure of flow paths, often including elevation and channel characteristics.

It may include:

  • channel centerlines
  • cross-sections
  • slope and elevation profiles

This is especially important for hydraulic modeling (e.g., flood analysis).

Time Series (flow over time)

Time series data represents how hydrologic variables change over time.

Examples:

  • streamflow (discharge)
  • precipitation
  • water level

The graph on the slide (flow vs. time) is an example of a hydrograph.

Linking spatial and temporal data

A key strength of Arc Hydro is linking:

  • geospatial data (where things are)
  • time series data (how things change over time)

For example:

  • a stream gauge (point) is linked to a time series of flow
  • a watershed is linked to precipitation records

This allows for dynamic analysis, not just static mapping.

Slide 38 Hydrology: Definition

On the slide

  • hy·drol·o·gy (hye-DROL-uh-jee)
  • noun
  • The scientific study of the properties, distribution, and effects of water on the earth's surface, in the soil and underlying rocks, and in the atmosphere.

Lecture notes

What is hydrology?

Hydrology is the scientific study of water—its properties, distribution, movement, and impacts across different parts of the Earth system.

This includes water in:

  • the atmosphere (e.g., precipitation, evaporation)
  • on the land surface (e.g., rivers, lakes, runoff)
  • in the soil (e.g., infiltration, soil moisture)
  • in underlying rocks (e.g., groundwater)

Hydrology looks at both where water is and how it moves and changes.

Key components of hydrology

Hydrology covers a wide range of processes, including:

  • Precipitation → rain, snow, and other forms of water entering the system
  • Infiltration → water moving into the soil
  • Runoff → water flowing over land into streams
  • Streamflow → movement of water through river systems
  • Groundwater flow → water movement below the surface
  • Evapotranspiration → water returning to the atmosphere

These processes are interconnected and form the hydrologic cycle.

Distribution of water

Hydrology also studies how water is distributed across space and time.

For example:

  • why some regions receive more rainfall than others
  • how water availability changes seasonally
  • how water is stored in snowpack, soil, or aquifers

This spatial variability is why GIS is such an important tool in hydrology.

Effects of water

Water has significant impacts on the environment and human systems.

Examples include:

  • shaping landscapes through erosion and sediment transport
  • influencing ecosystems and habitats
  • causing hazards such as floods and droughts
  • supporting water supply for agriculture, industry, and communities

Understanding these effects is a key goal of hydrologic analysis.

Slide 39 Arc Hydro Models Hydrology: The Water Cycle

Lecture notes

This USGS diagram of the water cycle shows the storages that hydrology studies (the atmosphere, ice and snow, oceans, lakes and rivers, and groundwater) and the fluxes between them (precipitation, evaporation, evapotranspiration, runoff, infiltration, and groundwater discharge). Arc Hydro represents many of these components in GIS so we can analyze them spatially.

Slide 40 Hydrography: Definition

On the slide

  • hy·drog·ra·phy (hye-DROG-ruh-fee)
  • noun
  • 1. The scientific description and analysis of the physical conditions, boundaries, flow, and related characteristics of the earth's surface waters.
  • 2. The mapping of bodies of water.

Lecture notes

What is hydrography?

Hydrography is the scientific description and mapping of surface water features on the Earth.

It focuses on:

  • the location of water bodies
  • their physical characteristics
  • how they are represented spatially

This includes features such as:

  • rivers and streams
  • lakes and reservoirs
  • wetlands
  • coastlines

Two key aspects of hydrography

1. Description and analysis of surface waters

Hydrography involves describing the physical properties of water features, such as:

  • boundaries (e.g., lake edges, riverbanks)
  • flow paths (stream channels)
  • connectivity between water bodies
  • characteristics such as width, depth, or classification

This is often based on mapped or observed data.

2. Mapping of water bodies

Hydrography is closely tied to cartography and GIS because it involves representing water features spatially.

In GIS, hydrography is typically stored as:

  • lines → rivers and streams
  • polygons → lakes, wetlands
  • points → monitoring stations or specific locations

These datasets are often compiled into standardized datasets (e.g., national hydrography databases).

Hydrography vs. Hydrology (important distinction)

Although the terms sound similar, they are different:

  • Hydrography
  • focuses on mapping and describing water features

answers: Where are the rivers and lakes?

Hydrology

focuses on processes and movement of water

answers: How does water move and change?

In GIS:

  • hydrography provides the data layers
  • hydrology provides the process understanding and analysis

Slide 41 Arc Hydro Represents Hydrography: Mapping Water Features

Lecture notes

Slide 42 Hydrology vs. Hydrography at a Glance

On the slide

AspectHydrologyHydrography
FocusProcesses and movement of waterLocation and description of water features
Key questionHow does water move and change?Where are the rivers, lakes, and wetlands?
Typical GIS dataRasters derived from a DEM (flow direction, flow accumulation); time seriesMapped vector features (streams, lakes, wetlands, gauges)
ExampleFlow accumulation grid computed from a DEMNational Hydrography Dataset (NHD) flowlines

Lecture notes

This table summarizes the distinction from the last few slides. Hydrology is about processes: how water moves and changes, which in GIS usually means rasters derived from a DEM, like flow direction and flow accumulation, plus time series such as streamflow. Hydrography is about mapped water features: where rivers, lakes, and wetlands are, usually stored as vector data such as NHD flowlines. A common mistake is to treat mapped hydrography as if it were the modeled flow path; the two often disagree, especially in flat terrain.

Slide 43 GIS Data Sources

On the slide

  • ArcGIS Living Atlas
  • Oregon Metro RLIS
  • Federal: NOAA, USGS, EPA, NAIP, NRCS, NWI, FEMA, BLM, USFS, Census
  • WA Dept. of Ecology
  • Oregon GEOHub

Lecture notes

ArcGIS Online – Atlas of the World

ArcGIS Online provides access to a large collection of global datasets, known as the “Atlas of the World.”

This includes:

  • basemaps (imagery, topography, streets)
  • environmental datasets
  • demographic data
  • ready-to-use web layers

This is often the easiest place to start when you need data quickly or want to explore available datasets.

Metro – local area data

Local or regional agencies (such as Metro in the Portland area) provide detailed datasets specific to a region.

These datasets often include:

  • high-resolution land use data
  • infrastructure (roads, utilities)
  • zoning and planning data
  • local environmental datasets

Local data is often more detailed and accurate than national datasets for a specific area.

Federal data sources (NOAA, USGS, EPA, etc.)

Many U.S. federal agencies provide high-quality, publicly available geospatial data.

Key agencies include:

  • NOAA → climate, precipitation, coastal data
  • USGS → elevation (DEMs), streamflow, hydrography (NHD)
  • EPA → water quality, watershed data
  • NRCS → soils, snowpack (SNOTEL)
  • NAIP → aerial imagery
  • FEMA → flood maps (FIRMs)
  • BLM / USFS → land management and natural resource data
  • Census → population and socioeconomic data

These sources are widely used in professional hydrology and environmental analysis.

State-level data (e.g., Washington Dept. of Ecology)

State agencies provide datasets tailored to regional conditions and regulatory needs.

Examples include:

  • water rights data
  • water quality monitoring
  • state-specific hydrography
  • regulatory and environmental datasets

These are especially important for applied projects and policy-related work.

Oregon Geospatial Data Clearinghouse

State data clearinghouses provide centralized access to GIS datasets.

For Oregon, this includes:

  • elevation and terrain data
  • hydrography and watershed boundaries
  • land use and land cover
  • environmental and infrastructure data

These portals are valuable for finding curated, standardized datasets.

Slide 44 Week 1 Key Takeaways

On the slide

  • Hydrology is inherently spatial; GIS shows where and how water moves
  • Data models abstract the real world: conceptual → mathematical → data → geographic
  • Vector suits discrete features; raster suits continuous surfaces; hydrology needs both
  • Core workflow: DEM → flow direction → flow accumulation → streams → watersheds
  • Always check projection, coordinate system, units, and metadata
  • Before next week: introduce yourself on Slack, complete the survey, and read the Hydrology toolset overview

Lecture notes

Five ideas to carry forward from Week 1. First, hydrology is inherently spatial, and GIS is how we analyze it. Second, working with data means moving through levels of abstraction, from the real world to a geographic data model. Third, vector and raster data each have a role, and hydrologic work needs both. Fourth, the core hydrologic GIS workflow starts from the DEM: flow direction, then flow accumulation, then streams and watersheds. Fifth, check your projection, units, and metadata every time. Before next week, introduce yourself on Slack, complete the survey, and read the Hydrology toolset overview.
